_notes: The years away at study: three in Rome for the licentiate in theology at the Gregorian, living at the graduate house of the North American College, or two in Washington for the canon law licentiate at the Catholic University. Phase is study; the engine sets study:rome or study:washington and provides the tokens {school}, {city}, {residence}. He has no parish and no pastor; the only selector is {@bishop}. Loneliness at Christmas, the Brookland rectory, and drink are authored only (no flavorPrompt). The credential italian is granted once, in st_rome_italian_oral. Flags written: study_italian_earned, study_exam_in_english, study_exam_in_latin, study_curial_backchannel, study_kept_clear_of_curia, study_thesis_bold, study_thesis_safe, study_spoke_plainly_at_table, study_talked_up_the_diocese, study_hosted_pilgrims, study_kept_the_rule, study_on_the_circuit, study_christmas_alone, study_christmas_served, study_christmas_with_strangers, study_sunday_supply, study_supply_limited, study_declined_supply, study_diocesan_errands, study_refused_errand, study_ticket_to_pilgrims, study_ticket_to_donor, study_met_the_pope, study_watched_the_drink, study_drank_in_rome, study_told_someone, study_guided_the_cardinal, study_gave_the_talk, study_recused, study_sat_on_home_case, study_blessed_the_office, study_blessed_on_camera, study_spoke_on_the_hill, study_rectory_useful, study_rectory_apart, study_found_company, study_told_bishop_anywhere, study_told_bishop_wish, study_bishop_named_his_plan, study_wrote_home.

events.title: Ten Minutes in Italian
events.body: The summer language course was six weeks of verbs in a hot classroom, and it got you as far as the bakery and the bus. Now it is January, and the examinations at {school} are oral, and the professor of dogmatic theology examines in Italian because that is the language of the house. You have ten minutes. He will ask about grace and the sacraments in the language of Dante, and you will answer in the language of a man who learned it from a workbook in August. The older priests at {residence} have told you the tricks: memorize the opening of each thesis, learn six connecting phrases, never stop talking. Some of them also told you the other trick, which is to ask to be examined in English, which the professors will permit and quietly remember. You stand in the corridor outside the aula with three Poles and a Nigerian, all of whom sound better than you. The door opens. He says your name, badly, and you go in.
events.flavorPrompt: The corridor, the door, the ten minutes; the small humiliations of a grown man learning to speak again.

choices.label: Take it in Italian and get through it however you can
choices.outcome: You do not stop talking. Half of it is grammar and half of it is nerve, and at one point you use the word for shepherd when you mean pastor, and he lets it pass. The grade is a grade. By Easter you are arguing with the porter about the football, and by June you can read the newspaper, which is the thing that actually matters.

choices.label: Ask, politely, to be examined in English
choices.outcome: He agrees at once, in an English better than your Italian will ever be, and the ten minutes go well. You know the material. The grade is good. In the refectory that evening one of the Poles asks how it went, and you tell him, and he says nothing at all, which is its own sentence. Your Italian stays at the level of the bakery.

choices.label: Offer to answer in Latin, since he prefers it to your Italian
choices.outcome: He looks at you over his glasses for a long moment and then says, in Latin, that this will be a pleasure. It is not a pleasure; it is the hardest ten minutes of your year. But he walks you to the door afterward, which he does for no one, and the story is around {residence} by supper. Your Italian is still no better than the bus.

effects.key: took his first Roman oral in Latin

events.title: A Word Carried Home
events.body: The monsignor is an American, twelve years in a dicastery near the Via della Conciliazione, with the good shoes and the tired courtesy of a man who has learned to say nothing in four languages. He finds you at a reception and knows your name and your diocese and the year you were ordained, and after the second glass he says there is a matter from {diocese} on his desk. He does not say what it is. He says it would go more easily if a certain letter from the chancery were withdrawn and resubmitted in different words, and that it would be a kindness to everyone if {@bishop} heard this from a son of the diocese rather than in an official reply that would have to be filed. He is not asking you to do anything improper. He is asking you to make a phone call. Everyone here makes phone calls. He gives you his card, which has no title on it, and moves on to the ambassador's wife.
events.flavorPrompt: The reception, the card with no title, the way Rome does its business sideways and calls it courtesy.

choices.label: Call the chancery and pass it along, exactly as he said it
choices.outcome: The chancellor listens, asks you to repeat it, and thanks you in the voice of a man writing things down. The letter is withdrawn. Whatever the matter was, it goes through. The monsignor nods to you at the next reception, which is how thanks are given here, and you understand that you have been added to a list you did not ask to join.

choices.label: Tell him it is not your place, and that the diocese has an address
choices.outcome: He smiles as if you have said something charming about the weather. Nothing changes in his manner and nothing is ever said again, and you are not invited to the next thing, or the one after. At home the official reply arrives in its own time, and the chancery does what chanceries do with official replies. No one knows what you declined.

choices.label: Call {@bishop} directly and let him decide what to do with it
choices.outcome: He picks up on the second ring, listens without interrupting, and asks two questions that tell you he knows exactly which matter it is. Then he says thank you, and that you did right to call him and not the office. The letter is withdrawn. He does not tell you what it was about, and you do not ask, and that is the whole transaction.

events.title: The Tesi
events.body: Your director at {school} is a Jesuit who has directed a hundred licentiate theses and remembers perhaps six. He reads your proposal in front of you, which takes four minutes, and then takes off his glasses. It is competent, he says. It will pass. It will be read by two examiners and then by no one. He has a different suggestion: take the second chapter, the one where you actually say something, and make it the whole thesis. It would mean a position. It would mean one of the examiners, whom he names, would fight you at the defense, and that the thesis would be talked about, which in Rome is a thing that happens to a man and not always a good one. Or, he says, putting the glasses back on, keep the proposal as it is. Get the degree. Go home. He has seen both kinds of men do well. He would like to know by Friday which kind you are.
events.flavorPrompt: The Jesuit's office, the glasses, a proposal read in four minutes; the moment a man decides what his name will be attached to.

choices.label: Take the second chapter and make it the whole thesis
choices.outcome: The examiner fights you, as promised, for forty minutes. You hold. The grade is a little lower than the safe thesis would have got, and a little higher than you feared, and two people you do not know ask for a copy. A monsignor at {residence} says, not unkindly, that he hopes you are not planning to be a bishop.

choices.label: Keep the proposal as it is and get the degree
choices.outcome: It passes, and passes well; the defense is cordial and short and the examiners go to lunch. The bound copy goes on a shelf in the library where it will be consulted by no one, and a second copy goes to {@bishop}, who writes a warm note. You have the degree, which is what you were sent for, and nothing attached to your name that anyone will have to explain.

choices.label: Write the bold one, and write it so well the examiner has nothing to hold
choices.outcome: The examiner comes to the defense with a page of objections and gets through three of them. On the fourth he stops, reads your footnote, and says, in Italian, that he withdraws the point. The director says nothing at all, which from him is a standing ovation. The thesis is talked about, and for once the talk is the right kind.

effects.key: defended a thesis Rome talked about

events.title: The Long Table
events.body: Thursday is the night the priests of the graduate house go up the hill to eat with the seminarians of {residence}, and you are placed, by someone who arranges these things, between two men from {diocese} in their second year and across from a guest. The guest is a monsignor from the Secretariat of State with a face you have seen in photographs behind other faces. Everyone at the table knows what everyone says, which is that he will have a diocese within five years, and that it will be an American one. The seminarians want to know about home: the parishes, the priests, whether it is true what they have heard about the finances and the closures and the man who left. They ask the way young men ask, as if there were a right answer. The monsignor eats slowly and does not appear to listen, in the way of a man who is listening to everything. What you say about {diocese} tonight will be repeated in two seminaries and one office, and you know it.
events.flavorPrompt: The refectory on the Janiculum, the seminarians' hunger for home, and the quiet guest who will remember every word.

choices.label: Tell them the truth about home, the good and the rest of it
choices.outcome: You tell them about the closures and the money and the man who left, and about the pastor who kept his parish alive on nothing and the deacon who buried half the town. The seminarians go quiet in the right way. The monsignor asks one question, precise and courteous, and then talks about the weather. Someone at home hears that you were candid. Someone else hears that you were loyal.

choices.label: Give them the diocese as the chancery would want it given
choices.outcome: You are warm and specific and leave out what should be left out, and the seminarians go to bed proud of a place they have not lived in since they were twenty. The monsignor says, on the stairs, that you speak well of your bishop, and it is not a question. Within the month {@bishop} has heard that you do.

choices.label: Turn the table's attention to the monsignor and ask him about Rome
choices.outcome: You ask him a real question about the Secretariat, one that shows you have been reading, and he answers it at length because no one at these dinners ever asks him anything. The seminarians get an hour on how the Church is actually run. He remembers you as the one who let him talk, which in his world is the highest form of intelligence.

events.title: Pilgrims from Home
events.body: The email comes from a travel agency and then from a parish secretary you half remember: forty-one pilgrims from {diocese} will be in Rome for four days, they have heard Father is studying there, and would he be free to say hello at St. Peter's on Tuesday. The list of names is attached. Halfway down it is the surname of {@bishop}, and it is his sister, who is a widow and a daily communicant and, by every account, the one person in the world he is afraid of. You have a seminar on Tuesday and a paper due Thursday. You also have a cassock, a working knowledge of the sacristy of the basilica, and the ability to get a Mass said at an altar in the grottoes for a group that will remember it for the rest of their lives. The parish secretary adds, in a second email, that they would be so grateful for anything at all, and that the bishop's sister has asked twice whether you are coming.
events.flavorPrompt: The pilgrims in the square, the bishop's sister among them, the exact weight of a Tuesday.

choices.label: Give them the whole day: the basilica, a Mass in the grottoes, dinner
choices.outcome: You skip the seminar. The Mass at the altar in the grottoes is at seven in the morning and half of them cry. You walk them through the basilica for three hours and the bishop's sister holds your arm on the stairs and tells you things about her brother that you will never repeat. The paper is late. The professor does not care. {@bishop} hears about the day before you are back at {residence}.

choices.label: Meet them in the square for an hour and go back to the library
choices.outcome: You shake forty-one hands in the colonnade and pose for the photograph and point at the dome. The bishop's sister is gracious and says she understands, Father has his studies, in a tone you will think about later. The paper is on time and good. Someone at home says the young priest in Rome was too busy for the pilgrims, and someone else says that is what he is there for.

choices.label: Use your Italian to get them where tourists do not go
choices.outcome: The sacristan owes you nothing but likes you, and the Mass is at the altar nearest the tomb. A friend in the Fabbrica walks them onto the roof. You translate for the widow who wants to light a candle for a husband dead thirty years, and for the bishop's sister, who wants to buy rosaries and argue about the price. She says, at the end, that her brother had better be good to you.

events.title: The Circuit
events.body: There is a Rome that happens after nine at night, and in your first months you did not know it existed. It is the dinner at the embassy to the Holy See where the ambassador's wife seats a young priest next to the guest she wants softened. It is the apartment near the Piazza Navona where a monsignor from a dicastery has the same eight people every Friday and a ninth chair for whoever is being tried out. It is the reception for a visiting archbishop, and the one for the new rector of somebody's college, and the one for no reason at all. The invitations began to arrive in the second month and now arrive every week. The graduate house of {residence} has a rule, an old and modest one, about being in the house by a certain hour and at Mass in the morning, and the men who keep it are not the men whose names come up when dioceses are discussed. The men who do not keep it have a look about them by the third year. You have seen both kinds on the stairs.
events.flavorPrompt: The lit windows near the Piazza Navona, the ninth chair, and the stairs of the house at midnight.

choices.label: Keep the rule of the house and let the invitations lapse
choices.outcome: The invitations thin out by Lent and stop by summer. You are at Mass every morning and at your desk every evening, and your Italian is better than that of men who have been here twice as long, because you use it on the porter and not on ambassadors. No one in the dicasteries knows your name. Some of the men on the stairs are visibly relieved.

choices.label: Go out, and learn how the city is actually run
choices.outcome: You learn who is in and who is out and why, and which monsignor is speaking to which, and that a dinner is a meeting with a tablecloth. You are tired in the mornings. Twice you miss Mass. The rector of the house says nothing, in a way that is a sentence, and a letter goes home that you will not read for years.

choices.label: Go out, and be the one they ask for again
choices.outcome: By spring the ambassador's wife asks for you by name. The Friday apartment gives you the ninth chair and then a regular one. You are useful at a table, which in this city is a career, and men who decide things begin to say your name to each other. Morning Mass becomes a thing you do most days. The thesis is late and nobody in the dicasteries minds.

events.title: Christmas in Rome
events.body: The house empties on the twentieth. The ones with money fly home. The ones with family in Europe go to them. The ones who are left are the Africans, two Poles, a man from Kerala, and you, and the refectory on the twenty-fourth seats eleven at tables built for eighty. You have a ticket for Midnight Mass at St. Peter's, obtained with some effort, and you go, and it is magnificent, and you are one of four thousand priests in choir dress, and you have never been so anonymous in your life. Afterward the buses have stopped. You walk back across the river at two in the morning past shuttered bars and a man sleeping on the steps of a church. In the morning there is the call home, which has to be timed to a house six hours behind you, where the dinner is at three and the dishes at five, and in which everyone passes the phone around and asks what it is like, and you say that it is beautiful, which is true. It is the twenty-fifth. You have nothing to do until the twenty-seventh.

choices.label: Say Mass alone in the house chapel and sit with it
choices.outcome: You say the Mass of Christmas Day at a side altar with no one there but a Polish priest who serves it and then says his own. Then you sit in the chapel for an hour. It is not a good hour and it is not a bad one; it is the hour that was there. In the afternoon you write a long letter to no one and do not send it.

choices.label: Go to the English-speaking parish and take whatever Masses they give you
choices.outcome: The pastor gives you the ten o'clock and the noon and a baptism at two, because his associate is in Ohio. The church is full of tourists and embassy families and Filipino nurses, and you preach the same homily three times and mean it three times. You are back at the house by four, tired in the ordinary way, which is the best way.

choices.label: Accept the invitation from the Italian family who feed the students
choices.outcome: The signora who runs the bar across the street has been asking for two weeks, and you go, and there are fourteen people in a flat built for five and a grandmother who holds your hand through the whole meal and tells you about her brother the priest, dead in 1971. You understand a third of it. You come home at nine, full, with a tin of something.

events.title: Sunday Supply
events.body: The English-speaking parish off the Via Veneto has a pastor who has been there twenty-two years and an associate who has just been recalled to Chicago, and the pastor finds you after a Sunday Mass at which you were a face in the pews. He needs supply. Just the ten o'clock, just for Advent, just until the province sends someone. You say yes, because a priest says yes. By Epiphany it is the ten o'clock and the noon. By Lent there are baptisms, and a wedding preparation for an embassy couple, and a funeral for a Filipino nurse whose family speak no Italian, and the pastor has begun to introduce you as his associate to people who do not know that you are not. He is a good priest and a lonely one and he has never let go of anything in his life. Your director at {school} has noticed that you look tired on Mondays. The pastor has an envelope for you every week that you have not asked for and cannot easily refuse.
events.flavorPrompt: The parish off the Via Veneto, the pastor who cannot let go, the envelope, the tired Mondays.

choices.label: Keep saying yes; this is what you were ordained for
choices.outcome: You are a parish priest again in everything but title and your thesis is a thing you do on Tuesdays. The embassy couple ask you to baptize the baby a year later. The pastor weeps when you leave, which you did not expect, and the diocese hears from an unlikely quarter that you are a pastor's pastor. The degree takes a little longer.

choices.label: Tell him plainly: one Sunday a month, and no more
choices.outcome: He takes it the way such men take it, which is with a wounded courtesy that lasts a month and then subsides into the arrangement. One Sunday a month you are useful and the other three you are a student. He never quite trusts you again and never quite lets you go either. It is, you will realize later, a rehearsal for every boundary you will ever have to draw.

choices.label: Step away entirely; you were sent here to study
choices.outcome: You write him a letter, because it is easier than saying it, and he replies with a letter that is gracious and a page too long. The province sends someone in June. You have your Sundays and your thesis moves. Two of the older priests at {residence} say, without saying it, that they would have found a way to do both.

events.title: A Small Thing, Since You Are There
events.body: The letter from the chancellor is two paragraphs long and begins with hoping Rome agrees with you. The second paragraph is the letter. A parish at home was suppressed last year, the people of it have taken recourse to the Dicastery for the Clergy against the decree, and the matter has been pending for eleven months. Since you are there, the chancellor writes, perhaps you could drop by the dicastery and see where things stand. Informally. He gives you the name of a monsignor and the protocol number. He does not say that you are being asked to become the diocese's man in Rome, or that the people who filed the recourse are people whose children you may have baptized, or that a student priest walking into a dicastery to ask about a pending case is a thing that is noticed and filed. He says it is a small thing. He signs it with his first name, which he has never done before, and adds that {@bishop} sends his regards.
events.flavorPrompt: The two-paragraph letter, the protocol number, the word informally doing all the work.

choices.label: Go, ask politely where it stands, and report back only what you are told
choices.outcome: The monsignor receives you for six minutes, tells you the case is under study, and says the diocese's position is understood. It is what he would have told anyone. You write it back in three lines. The chancellor replies that this is very helpful, and it is: the diocese now has a face in the building, and the face is yours, and there will be another letter.

choices.label: Write back that a student has no business lobbying a dicastery
choices.outcome: You say it as gently as it can be said and it is still a refusal. The chancellor does not reply. The matter is decided eleven months later, as it would have been, and you learn the result from the diocesan paper. Two priests at home hear what you declined and think better of you; the chancery hears it and files it under something.

choices.label: Ask someone you actually know in the building where it really stands
choices.outcome: Over lunch, a friend of a friend tells you which desk it is on and what that desk usually does, and that the diocese's brief was thin in one place he names. You write home what you have learned, carefully. The chancellor calls you, which has never happened, and the brief is quietly supplemented. Your friend of a friend does not mention it again, and you owe him.

events.title: One Ticket
events.body: The house gets an allocation for the Wednesday audience, and once a year, by a rotation nobody understands, a priest of the graduate house is given a single place in the front section, the one from which, if the Holy Father comes down the line, a man may shake his hand and say two sentences. The rector hands you the envelope on Monday. By Monday night three people want it. A couple from your old parish, retired, are in Rome on the trip of their lives and wrote to you a month ago asking only whether you might have coffee. A monsignor you know slightly from a dicastery has a donor in town, a serious one, and has asked, in the way he asks things, whether you might have something for him. And you have never met a pope. You have been a priest for years and you have never been closer than a piazza and a screen, and it is Wednesday in two days, and the envelope is on your desk.
events.flavorPrompt: The envelope on the desk, the three claims on it, the two sentences a man gets to say.

choices.label: Give it to the couple from home
choices.outcome: The wife cries in the square before anything has happened. The Holy Father comes down the line and takes her hand and she says her two sentences, and the husband takes the photograph that will be on their wall until they die. They tell the whole parish. Someone tells {@bishop}. The monsignor, when you see him next, does not mention it, which is how he mentions it.

choices.label: Give it to the monsignor for his donor
choices.outcome: The donor gets his handshake and his photograph and the monsignor gets whatever he was going to get, and a month later a check arrives at the chancery at home with a note that mentions you. The couple from your old parish have coffee with you on Thursday and are glad of it. You do not tell them what Wednesday was.

choices.label: Go yourself; you may never have another chance
choices.outcome: He is smaller than you expected and his hand is warm and you say the two sentences you rehearsed, and he says something back you will spend years trying to remember exactly. You are a priest who has met the pope. The couple have their coffee. The monsignor finds another ticket. You are not sorry, and you notice that you are not.

effects.key: shook the pope's hand in the front row

events.title: The Roman Evening
events.body: It is not any one thing. It is wine at lunch because the house serves wine at lunch. It is the aperitivo at seven because the man from Kerala likes company and the bar is across the street. It is the grappa the porter's cousin brings at Christmas and the bottle a monsignor left in the common room and the digestivo that arrives at the end of every dinner in this city whether you ask for it or not. It is the fact that the evenings are long and the room is small and the thesis is not going well, and that a glass makes the thesis matter less, and that two makes the room bigger. None of the men on the stairs would call it a problem. Some of the men on the stairs have been here nine years. You noticed, last Tuesday, that you were counting the hours until seven, and you noticed that you noticed, and then you had the glass anyway, and it was fine, and it is always fine, and that is the thing about it.

choices.label: Set a rule for yourself and keep it, quietly
choices.outcome: One glass at dinner and nothing after Compline. The first two weeks are longer than you expected and the third is ordinary. Nobody notices, because you make sure nobody notices. The thesis does not get better and the room does not get bigger, but you are the one deciding what the evening is, which is the point.

choices.label: Let it be what it is; everyone here drinks, and you are fine
choices.outcome: You are fine. You are good company at seven and better at ten, and the men who have been here nine years like you, and the evenings pass. In the spring you say a Mass with a headache you had not planned and it goes well, and you note that it went well, and you put the note somewhere you will find it later.

choices.label: Say it out loud to the spiritual director of the house
choices.outcome: He is an old Sulpician who has heard everything and reacts as if you have described the weather, which is what you needed. He asks three questions and gives you nothing to sign. You see him every two weeks for the rest of the year. The bar across the street is still there. So is he.

effects.key: asked for help before he needed it

events.title: The Cardinal's Week
events.body: An American cardinal is coming for eight days, with a priest secretary who has never been to Rome and a lay staff of four who have never been anywhere, and the rector of {residence} has been asked to find them a priest who knows the city and the language and can be trusted at a table. He has proposed you. It means a week of restaurants and doorways and knowing which entrance to the Palazzo to use, and it means sitting in on things a student does not usually sit in on. It also means the last night, when the cardinal is hosting sixty American donors and journalists at a hotel on the Via Veneto, and his secretary has asked whether you would give the after-dinner talk, twenty minutes, on the Church in America as a young priest sees it. On the record. The cardinal has a known line on how a diocese should be governed, and his secretary has, very kindly, sent you three of his speeches. {@bishop}, you are aware, has a line of his own.
events.flavorPrompt: Eight days of doorways and restaurants, the secretary's kindness with the speeches, and the hotel ballroom on the last night.

choices.label: Do the week, and give the talk they are hoping for
choices.outcome: You give twenty good minutes on unity behind the bishop and the dangers of a Church governed by committee, and the room stands, and a journalist quotes you in a piece that is read at home. The cardinal calls you by your first name. {@bishop} reads the piece and is not entirely sure it was about him. Your name is now on a side, and you did not choose the side; you chose the ballroom.

choices.label: Do the week, and give the talk you actually believe
choices.outcome: You give twenty minutes on a Church that listens before it governs, and the room is polite, and the cardinal is gracious in the way of a man crossing something off. The journalist quotes you at length. The secretary does not write again. At home, priests who never noticed you begin to, and {@bishop} says nothing, which from him could be anything.

choices.label: Do the week, and decline the talk; you are a student, not a spokesman
choices.outcome: The secretary is disappointed for exactly one conversation and then has a monsignor give the talk, which is what he would have done anyway. You spend eight days learning the city from the inside and are thanked warmly and privately. Nothing is quoted. The cardinal's office knows your name, which is worth something, and nobody at home knows anything, which is worth something else.

events.title: A Name You Know
events.body: The practicum at the archdiocesan tribunal is where the canons you have been reading at {school} become people. Mostly it is marriage cases: the petition, the witnesses, the long typed depositions in which a whole life is reduced to whether a man meant it at twenty-three. This week the judicial vicar hands you a rogatory commission. The tribunal of {diocese} has a witness living in Washington and has asked this tribunal to take her testimony, and he would like you to conduct it, since you know the diocese and it will be good practice. You open the file. The petitioner is a woman whose daughter you prepared for First Communion. The respondent is a man who ushered at the eight o'clock. The witness is his sister. Nobody here knows this, and nobody would, and the deposition would be perfectly proper in every way that could be written down. The judicial vicar is already on to the next file. It is your name on the commission.
events.flavorPrompt: The typed depositions, the file that opens onto a face from home, the judicial vicar already on to the next thing.

choices.label: Tell the judicial vicar you know the parties and step aside
choices.outcome: He looks up, nods once, and gives it to the other student, and it is over in ninety seconds. He does not say well done, because in his world it is not remarkable, only necessary. Weeks later he gives you a harder case than you were due, and you understand that it is the same sentence, said differently.

effects.key: recused himself when no one would have known

choices.label: Take it; you know the diocese, and that is why he gave it to you
choices.outcome: The sister is precise and sad and says things about her brother that you did not know and cannot now not know. The deposition is competent and goes home under seal. Nothing improper is written anywhere. You will be back in {diocese} in a year, and one Sunday the usher from the eight o'clock will shake your hand, and you will know what you know.

choices.label: Call the judicial vicar at home and have him redirect it himself
choices.outcome: He remembers you, and is briefly annoyed at himself for not checking, and sends a corrected commission naming the other student by return. The Washington tribunal never has to know why. At home, the judicial vicar mentions to the vicar general that the young man in Washington has a head for procedure, which is the kind of remark that gets a man a desk someday.

events.title: A Blessing on the Hill
events.body: The staffer is thirty, from a parish in Northern Virginia where you helped out one Sunday, and he has your number because you gave it to him. His member has new offices in one of the House buildings, the staff are mostly Catholic, and would Father come and bless the suite. There would be a few people from the press, because there always are, and the member would be there. You look the member up, which you should have done before you said maybe. His whole public life is one issue, and the issue is immigration, and his position on it is the reason he is in Congress. A priest in a collar in that doorway with holy water is not a house blessing. It is a photograph, and the photograph will be read in {diocese} by people who baptize their children in Spanish and by people who do not, and by {@bishop}, who has a position of his own and a diocese that does not agree with itself. The staffer says the member is really looking forward to it. He says Thursday at four.
events.flavorPrompt: The House office building, the holy water, the doorway that is really a photograph.

choices.label: Bless the offices on a quiet morning, no press, no member
choices.outcome: You come at eight on a Tuesday, when the member is in committee, and bless the rooms and the twelve staff who are there, and it is what a blessing is supposed to be. The staffer is a little disappointed and mostly grateful. No photograph exists. Someone in the member's office tells someone that the priest was decent about it, which is the only review you get.

choices.label: Do it Thursday at four, as asked, and keep it to the rite
choices.outcome: The blessing takes four minutes and the photographs take ten. You say nothing but the prayers. It does not matter: the picture runs, and in it you are standing beside the member, and a picture does not carry a caption saying that you only said the prayers. At home the Spanish Masses hear about it first. {@bishop} does not call, which is a kind of call.

choices.label: Go, bless the offices, and say a word about the stranger at the gate while the cameras are on
choices.outcome: You bless the rooms and then, with the member beside you and the cameras on, you say three sentences about the stranger and the gate and who the Church has always said he is. The member's smile does not move. The clip runs. The staffer does not call again. At home, one deanery is proud of you and another is not, and the chancery has a file with your name on it that did not exist on Wednesday.

events.title: A Room in Brookland
events.body: {residence} was full, or the diocese preferred the cheaper arrangement, and so you have a room on the third floor of a rectory in Brookland, six blocks from {school}, for which {diocese} sends the pastor a check every month. He is seventy-one and kind and has had student priests in that room for twenty years, and he is not interested in you. He eats at six, alone, with the television. The associate is Nigerian and out every evening at a mission he runs somewhere in Maryland. The housekeeper leaves at three. You come home from the library at nine to a dark house and a plate in the refrigerator with your name on it in marker, and you eat it standing up, and you go upstairs. At home you had a parish, and a parish is noise: the phone, the door, the man at the back after Mass who needed twenty minutes. Here no one needs twenty minutes. Nobody calls the third floor. You have never had so much time and you are not sure, some nights, what a priest is for without anyone in the room.

choices.label: Make yourself useful in the house: take a Mass, take the door, sit with him at six
choices.outcome: You take the six-thirty on Wednesdays and Fridays and start eating at six with the television, and after three weeks he turns it down, and after six he turns it off. He tells you about a parish in 1979. You are still a lodger, but you are a lodger he waits for. The dark house is a house.

choices.label: Keep to the third floor and the library; this is what the time is for
choices.outcome: You read more in a year than in the seven before it. The canons stop being a wall and become a building with doors. You are first in your cohort at {school} and the professors know it. The pastor and you exchange perhaps forty sentences between September and May, and the plate is always there, and you are always grateful, and you are always alone.

choices.label: Find the other student priests and make a Thursday of it
choices.outcome: There are nine of you scattered in rectories and at {residence}, from seven dioceses, and a Jesuit who cooks. Thursdays become dinner at whoever's house has the biggest table. It is not a parish. It is priests being priests to each other, which you did not know you needed until the second Thursday, when you were the last to leave.

events.title: The Bishop Calls
events.body: He calls at an hour that is convenient for him, and asks how it goes, and listens to the answer for longer than you expected, and then there is a pause in which you can hear him deciding how much to say. He has not sent a priest away to study for nothing; men do not go to {school} at the diocese's expense so that they can come home and be good at parish festivals. He does not say what he wants you for. He says that the chancellor is not young, and that the seminary faculty is thin, and that the tribunal has had a lay judge doing the work of three priests since the spring, and that he has been thinking about the future, which is the kind of sentence a bishop says when the future has a name in it. Then he asks whether there is anything you want him to know. It is a real question and it is also a door, and behind the door is the rest of your life in {diocese}, and he is waiting on the line from six time zones away.
events.flavorPrompt: The long-distance pause, the bishop's list of empty chairs, the question that is also a door.

choices.label: Tell him you will go wherever he sends you
choices.outcome: He says good, in a voice that has heard it before and believes it from perhaps one man in three, and then he says he thinks you mean it. The call ends warmly. You have given him the thing bishops most want and least often get, and you have given away the only moment in which you might have asked for something.

choices.label: Tell him plainly what you would want, and what you would not
choices.outcome: You say it in three sentences, and there is a silence, and then he says that he appreciates knowing. He does not say yes and he does not say no. A bishop who knows what a man wants can give it to him or withhold it, and you have handed him both keys; but he will never be able to say you did not tell him.

choices.label: Ask him, since he has raised it, what he has in mind for you
choices.outcome: He laughs, once, and then tells you, because you have earned it and because he is tired of carrying it alone. It is a real plan, with a year attached, and it is more than you expected, and he asks you not to repeat it. You will not. For the rest of your time away you are studying for something with a shape, and it changes how you read.

events.title: A Letter from Home
events.body: It is an actual letter, on parish stationery, four pages in the hand of a man you were ordained beside, who was never a writer and has clearly sat down at a kitchen table on a Sunday night to do this on purpose. He is a vicar in a parish you know, and the news is the news: the old pastor of the cathedral is dead and the funeral was enormous; two parishes in the north of the diocese have been put under one man, who is drowning; a classmate of yours has gone quiet and nobody can get him on the phone; the chancery has a new chancellor's assistant who is twenty-nine and already feared. And then a paragraph about you. They talk about you, he says. The men at the deanery meetings say the bishop has plans for you, and they say it the way priests say things, half proud and half something else, and he thought you should know. He signs it with his first name and a request: write back. Not an email. A letter. He wants to know what {city} is actually like.
events.flavorPrompt: Four handwritten pages on parish stationery, the deanery gossip, the classmate who cannot be reached.

choices.label: Write back at length, four pages of your own, the truth of it
choices.outcome: You write about the exams and the loneliness and what {city} smells like at seven in the morning, and about what you miss, which is the man at the back of church after Mass. He reads it to two other classmates at a dinner. It is passed around. A year later, when you come home, three men you barely knew greet you as if you had never left.

choices.label: Send a card with a few lines and get back to the reading
choices.outcome: The card says that you are well and working hard and that you will see him at Christmas or the one after, and it is true. He does not write again, not from any grievance, but because letters are hard and yours did not ask for one. The chapter you were reading is finished that night. The diocese hears nothing from you until you are back in it.

choices.label: Call him, tonight, and ask about the classmate nobody can reach
choices.outcome: He picks up in his car and talks for forty minutes. The quiet classmate has been drinking, or has stopped believing, or both, and nobody has driven out there, and by the end of the call your classmate has said he will go on Tuesday. He goes. It is not fixed. It is visited. He tells the others you were the one who asked.
